If a home loan costs 8% while an SIP/savings investment earns 12%, shouldn’t we compare the returns after tax? At a 30% tax rate, that 12% becomes roughly 8.4%, so at some point, aren’t the two almost equivalent?

If an 8% home loan is spread over 20 years, is there a point—say, when only 8 years are left—where it actually makes more sense *not* to prepay the loan and instead keep the money invested? In the last few years, aren’t we already paying mostly principal with relatively little interest?

My suggestion would be to aggressively pay down the home loan only while the interest component is high, especially since it’s a floating-rate loan. Once you reach the later years, the math may not justify paying it off completely.

This is what I did: I took a ₹20 lakh personal loan for one year at 11.5% and used it to prepay my home loan. The reduction in home-loan interest saved me several lakhs, even after accounting for the interest I paid on the personal loan. Now, with the home loan further along, I’m mostly paying principal.

I agree this strategy isn’t practical or suitable for everyone. But my point is: the goal doesn’t necessarily have to be to pay off the home loan completely. It may make more sense to optimize the interest burden early, and then let the remaining loan run while your money stays invested.

Equity returns cannot be predicted with certainty. In a major market crash, your portfolio can fall substantially, and if you are forced to withdraw at that time, your capital can take a serious hit.

Gold is also not a simple alternative, especially when the dollar is strengthening and gold prices are already high.

But one important value of a plot is being overlooked: land has utility value, not just investment value. A plot can be used for farming, horticulture, rental/commercial activities, or even to start a business. The income generated from such productive use can potentially be far greater than what a passive investment can provide.

And calling a 20-year mutual-fund CAGR “liquidity” is misleading. Liquidity simply means you can sell and access the money—not that you will get a guaranteed return. If you need the money after, say, 13 years, the market could be down at that particular time and your actual return could even be negative.

So the comparison should not be only about CAGR. Risk, timing of withdrawal, utility, cash flow potential and real-world use of the asset also matter.If you want, I can make it more aggressive/debatable, like a direct reply to someone arguing in favour of mutual funds.

•	Highlights: Limited supply makes it a powerful long-term store of value; prices are not checked daily, helping with investor discipline.

•	Highlights: Provides mental peace and financial security by removing debt.
